hook: We save more than ever, yet what we saved rarely resurfaces at the moment it could help.
lede: We encounter too much fragmented information, save the useful parts across different platforms, and then struggle to find them again. Notebooks and note-taking apps store it all and do little with it, and today’s generative AI tools, however capable, each work inside their own silo. Brain Cache is a position paper that asks what would change if generative AI acted not as another assistant but as a cognitive exoskeleton: a second brain that externalizes, structures and activates what we know.

stats.label: interlocked crises: overloaded memory, fragmented thinking, inert knowledge
capture channels: conscious outputs and subconscious interaction
mechanisms in one loop: externalize, structure, activate

chapters.title: Saved somewhere, found nowhere
paragraphs: The paper calls the condition cognitive entropy: biological memory overwhelmed by a deluge of data, thinking fragmented across discontinuous digital contexts, and critical knowledge that stays inert despite being technically stored. Traditional tools, from notebooks to note-taking apps, work as passive storage rather than active partners.

Generative AI looks like a remedy, but today it arrives as islands: writing assistants, design tools that synthesize mood boards, research accelerators, each confined to its own application. These systems excel at doing-for-thinking, automating cognitive labor, but neglect thinking-for-thinking: proactively restructuring what a person knows.

quote.text: This gap between information availability and actionable knowledge creates a paradoxical “cognitive poverty in the age of abundance”.

figures.caption: From the talk: fragmented information, scattered across platforms, saved somewhere but hard to find again.

chapters.title: Capture the thinking, not just the notes
paragraphs: The idea builds on extended cognition. Sparrow et al. found that people prioritize remembering where information is stored over what it contains, suggesting the brain already treats external repositories as memory. Brain Cache takes this further with two capture channels. The explicit channel records deliberate outputs such as research notes, annotated diagrams and lecture recordings, gathered through phones, augmented reality glasses and neural-textile sensors and tagged with location, collaboration session and timestamp.

The implicit channel continuously follows spontaneous cognitive activity: interaction records, eye-tracking heatmaps and EEG patterns from non-invasive biosensors. Merged, the two channels form a vector space meant to preserve the continuity of thought, linking deliberate intellectual work with subconscious activity.

figures.caption: Externalization: an explicit channel of conscious outputs and an implicit channel of subconscious interaction, merged into one vector space.

chapters.title: Knowledge that finds you first
paragraphs: Structuring turns these traces into a cognitive graph that keeps evolving. Rather than grouping concepts by semantic proximity, RAG-enhanced construction links them by the causal and temporal relationships in the user’s own decision history. Chain-of-Thought analysis then uncovers implicit reasoning paths, and an error-correction protocol flags inconsistencies such as circular reasoning or flawed experimental designs, offering scaffolding prompts and alternative frameworks.

Activation is where the graph pays off. Predictive models map current cognitive-load patterns to likely needs and surface related memories before the user searches for them, and retrieval adapts to each person’s cognitive style. The system does not only answer: it offers hints and suggestions that challenge the user’s thinking. Knowledge gains weight as it proves useful, and when the user hits a barrier, both channels are searched just in time.

figures.caption: Structuring: RAG construction, Chain-of-Thought analysis and error correction iterate around a graph database, organizing chaotic nodes into a causal chain.

chapters.title: A second brain, and its price
paragraphs: The three mechanisms form a loop. Externalized traces feed the graph, the graph informs activation, and applying knowledge creates new experiences that are captured again. The paper likens this cycle to biological neuroplasticity and calls it “cognitive metabolism”: raw experience digested into structured knowledge that shapes how new information is taken in.

The same intimacy creates the risks. Continuous capture of implicit memory opens uncharted territory in neuroprivacy and demands new frameworks for cognitive data ownership. Prolonged use could gradually reshape a person’s native reasoning patterns, enhancing or constraining cognitive diversity, and reliance on wearable sensors ties the vision to progress in miniaturizing neural interfaces.

quote.text: Does optimal augmentation require seamless integration with biological processes, or should deliberate friction be maintained to preserve metacognitive awareness?

takeaways: Personal knowledge tools could move from passive storage to active partners that structure and resurface what we know.
Organizing knowledge by a person’s own causal and temporal history, rather than folders and tags, would bring a second brain closer to how memory associates.
The closer AI gets to our thinking, the more pressing questions of neuroprivacy, dependency and cognitive ownership become.
